blocks.text: A 61-year-old woman, nine years past her menopause, notices pink staining on the tissue paper on two occasions. She is slightly embarrassed and nearly does not mention it. Her bleeding is the one symptom that makes endometrial cancer visible early, and most women with it are cured. A different woman, with months of bloating and early satiety that were put down to irritable bowel syndrome, has a cancer that typically presents when it has already spread. This unit contrasts these two diseases and what makes the difference.

blocks.markdown:
**Postmenopausal bleeding (PMB)** is any vaginal bleeding occurring 12 months or more after the last menstrual period. It is never normal and should be investigated, although most causes are benign. The commonest cause is **atrophic vaginitis or endometrial atrophy** (thin, oestrogen-deficient tissue). Other causes: endometrial or cervical polyps, endometrial hyperplasia, **endometrial cancer** (found in roughly 5 to 10% of women with PMB), hormone therapy, **tamoxifen** (a partial oestrogen agonist at the endometrium, causing polyps, hyperplasia and cancer), cervical cancer, vulval or vaginal lesions, and non-gynaecological bleeding from the urethra or rectum.

**Risk factors for endometrial cancer** reflect exposure to **unopposed oestrogen**: obesity (peripheral conversion of androstenedione to oestrone in adipose tissue), nulliparity, early menarche and late menopause, polycystic ovary syndrome and chronic anovulation, oestrogen-only hormone therapy in a woman with a uterus, tamoxifen, and diabetes. Lynch syndrome (hereditary non-polyposis colorectal cancer) greatly increases lifetime risk. **Type 1** tumours (endometrioid, oestrogen-related, usually low grade) are the majority; **type 2** tumours (serous, clear cell) are not oestrogen-driven and carry a worse prognosis.

**Investigating PMB.** Examine the abdomen, vulva, vagina (speculum for atrophy, polyps or a cervical lesion) and cervix, with bimanual examination. UK pathways treat PMB in women aged 55 or over as a suspected cancer referral. First-line imaging is **transvaginal ultrasound (TVUS)** to measure endometrial thickness; a thickness of **4 mm or less** has a very low risk of cancer (check local thresholds). A thicker endometrium, or persistent or recurrent bleeding despite a thin one, requires **hysteroscopy with directed biopsy** (or outpatient endometrial sampling) to obtain histology, because ultrasound alone cannot diagnose cancer. Women on tamoxifen with bleeding need hysteroscopic assessment because the endometrium is often thickened by benign change.

**Management of endometrial cancer** depends on histology and stage (FIGO): stage I confined to the uterine body; II cervical stroma involved; III local and regional spread; IV bladder, bowel or distant disease. Standard treatment is **total hysterectomy with bilateral salpingo-oophorectomy**, with lymph node assessment in selected cases, and adjuvant radiotherapy or chemotherapy for higher-risk disease. Because most cases present early with bleeding, five-year survival for stage I disease is high.

rows: Persistent bloating, early satiety, pelvic pain, urinary frequency (vague)
Most often stage III or IV
TVUS endometrial thickness, then hysteroscopy and biopsy
CA125 and pelvic ultrasound, then Risk of Malignancy Index
Unopposed oestrogen: obesity, nulliparity, PCOS, tamoxifen, Lynch syndrome
Older age, BRCA1 and BRCA2 mutations, Lynch syndrome, nulliparity, endometriosis
Surgical staging and cytoreduction with platinum-based chemotherapy

blocks.title: Working through a case of postmenopausal bleeding
blocks.prompt: A 64-year-old woman (BMI 36, type 2 diabetes, nulliparous) has had three episodes of fresh vaginal bleeding in 2 months, 13 years after her menopause. She is not on hormonal therapy. Speculum examination shows an atrophic-looking vagina and normal cervix. TVUS shows an endometrial thickness of 11 mm. Outline the next steps.

steps.text: Risk assessment: obesity, diabetes and nulliparity are all risk factors for unopposed oestrogen exposure, so the pre-test probability of endometrial cancer is raised. Bleeding more than 12 months after menopause fits the definition of PMB, so a suspected cancer referral applies.
Interpret the scan: an endometrial thickness of 11 mm greatly exceeds the 4 mm threshold associated with very low cancer risk, so tissue diagnosis is required.

Next step: hysteroscopy with directed biopsy. If histology confirms endometrial cancer, MRI or CT evaluates the extent, and treatment is usually total hysterectomy with bilateral salpingo-oophorectomy, with adjuvant therapy determined by stage and grade.

blocks.answer: Urgent hysteroscopy with biopsy, because the 11 mm endometrium is above the 4 mm threshold; the findings determine staging and surgery.

blocks.markdown:
**Ovarian mass.** Presentations range from incidental findings to acute pain (torsion, rupture) to the **symptoms of ovarian cancer**: persistent abdominal distension or bloating, early satiety or loss of appetite, pelvic or abdominal pain, and urinary urgency or frequency, with weight loss and changes in bowel habit. Women aged 50 or over with new symptoms resembling irritable bowel syndrome should have ovarian cancer considered. The commonest malignant type is **epithelial ovarian cancer** (high-grade serous carcinoma is most frequent); **germ cell tumours** (for example dysgerminoma) occur in young women, and **sex cord-stromal tumours** (granulosa cell) are rare.

**Assessment.** Examination may reveal a pelvic mass, ascites or an omental mass. **CA125** (a glycoprotein marker) and **pelvic ultrasound** are first-line tests; CA125 is raised in many ovarian cancers but also in benign conditions (endometriosis, fibroids, pelvic inflammation, menstruation, pregnancy and cirrhosis), so it supports risk assessment rather than diagnosing. In young women with a complex mass, check **alpha-fetoprotein (AFP), beta-hCG and LDH** for germ cell tumours. The **Risk of Malignancy Index (RMI)** combines three components, shown below; an RMI over 250 suggests a high risk and warrants referral to a gynaecological oncology multidisciplinary team. Management of cancer is **surgical staging and cytoreduction** (hysterectomy, bilateral salpingo-oophorectomy, omentectomy, removal of visible disease) with platinum-based chemotherapy, and maintenance therapy (for example PARP inhibitors in BRCA-mutated tumours).

blocks.caption: U = ultrasound score (0 for none, 1 for one, 3 for two or more of: multilocular cyst, solid areas, bilateral lesions, ascites, intra-abdominal metastases); M = menopausal status (1 premenopausal, 3 postmenopausal); CA125 in U/mL. RMI above 250 is high risk.

blocks.title: Calculating the Risk of Malignancy Index
blocks.prompt: A 58-year-old postmenopausal woman has a complex pelvic mass with multilocular cysts and solid areas, with ascites on ultrasound. CA125 is 340 U/mL. Calculate the RMI and state the action.

steps.text: Ultrasound score: she has three features (multilocular, solid areas, ascites). Two or more features give U = 3.
RMI = U x M x CA125 = 3 x 3 x 340 = 3,060. This is well above 250, so refer to the gynaecological oncology multidisciplinary team for staging imaging and surgery rather than local management.

blocks.answer: RMI = 3,060, high risk; refer to a gynaecological oncology MDT.

blocks.markdown: **Why ovarian cancer is diagnosed late.** Several factors combine: (1) **non-specific symptoms** (bloating, early satiety, urinary frequency) that mimic irritable bowel syndrome, dyspepsia and ageing, so they are often attributed to benign causes and the diagnosis is delayed; (2) the ovary sits deep in the pelvis, so small tumours produce no signs and are not palpable; (3) the cancer spreads by **transcoelomic (peritoneal) shedding** and implantation on the peritoneum and omentum, so cells disseminate early without any anatomical barrier; (4) there is **no effective screening test**: CA125 with ultrasound has not been shown to reduce deaths in the general population, and CA125 lacks specificity; and (5) the peak incidence is in older women with other comorbidities. Consequently most women present with stage III or IV disease and survival is lower than in endometrial cancer.

items: Any bleeding after 12 months of amenorrhoea needs investigation by TVUS and, if indicated, hysteroscopy with biopsy.
The commonest cause of PMB is atrophy; the most important cause to exclude is endometrial cancer.
Tamoxifen increases the risk of endometrial polyps, hyperplasia and cancer.
CA125 is a risk marker, not a diagnostic test; use RMI for risk stratification.
Persistent bloating, early satiety, pelvic pain or urinary frequency in a woman over 50 should prompt CA125 and ultrasound.

blocks.title: A thin endometrium does not close the case if bleeding persists
blocks.text: A reassuringly thin endometrium on ultrasound lowers the risk of endometrial cancer, but women with recurrent or persistent PMB, or those on tamoxifen, still need hysteroscopic assessment. Ovarian cancer should also be considered whenever a woman over 50 has persistent bloating or early satiety, even if the endometrium looks normal.

points: Postmenopausal bleeding is investigated with TVUS endometrial thickness and hysteroscopy with biopsy when indicated; atrophy is the commonest cause and endometrial cancer the most important.
Endometrial cancer is linked to unopposed oestrogen and presents early, so most women are cured by hysterectomy and bilateral salpingo-oophorectomy.
An ovarian mass is assessed with CA125, ultrasound and the Risk of Malignancy Index; high-risk women are managed by a gynaecological oncology MDT.
Ovarian cancer is diagnosed late because of vague symptoms, deep location, early peritoneal spread and absence of an effective screening test.

questions.stem: What is the most common cause of postmenopausal bleeding?

options.text: Atrophic vaginitis or endometrial atrophy
Endometrial cancer
Cervical cancer
Uterine fibroids

distractorRationale.a: Correct: oestrogen deficiency makes tissues thin and fragile.
distractorRationale.b: Endometrial cancer is important but responsible for only a minority of cases.
distractorRationale.c: Cervical cancer is a less common cause.
distractorRationale.d: Fibroids shrink after menopause and rarely cause postmenopausal bleeding.

questions.explanation: Atrophy is the most common cause but is a diagnosis of exclusion; cancer must be considered in every woman. The risk that bleeding represents cancer is the reason all PMB is investigated.

questions.stem: A 59-year-old woman not on hormone therapy has a single episode of postmenopausal bleeding. Transvaginal ultrasound shows an endometrial thickness of 3 mm. Which management is most appropriate?

options.text: Reassure, treat any vaginal atrophy, and advise prompt re-referral if bleeding recurs
Immediate hysterectomy
Pelvic MRI and CA125 only
Start oestrogen-only HRT

questions.correctOptionText: Reassure, treat any vaginal atrophy, and advise prompt re-referral if bleeding recurs

distractorRationale.a: Correct: a thin endometrium has a very low cancer risk; recurrence needs hysteroscopy.
distractorRationale.c: MRI and CA125 have no role in this scenario.
distractorRationale.d: Unopposed oestrogen in a woman with a uterus raises cancer risk.

questions.explanation: An endometrial thickness at or below 4 mm carries a very low risk of cancer, so a single episode with this finding can be managed conservatively. Persistent or recurrent bleeding requires hysteroscopy because ultrasound can miss focal lesions.

questions.stem: A 66-year-old woman taking tamoxifen for breast cancer reports vaginal bleeding. Which statement best explains why she needs hysteroscopic assessment?

options.text: Tamoxifen acts as a partial oestrogen agonist on the endometrium, raising the risk of polyps, hyperplasia and cancer
Tamoxifen causes endometrial atrophy, so bleeding is always benign
Tamoxifen only affects the breast and has no uterine effects
Tamoxifen is a progestogen that protects the endometrium

questions.correctOptionText: Tamoxifen acts as a partial oestrogen agonist on the endometrium, raising the risk of polyps, hyperplasia and cancer

distractorRationale.a: Correct: tamoxifen is an oestrogen antagonist in breast tissue but an agonist in the endometrium.
distractorRationale.b: It stimulates, rather than atrophies, the endometrium.
distractorRationale.d: It is a selective oestrogen receptor modulator, not a progestogen.

questions.explanation: Tamoxifen has tissue-specific actions: it blocks oestrogen receptors in breast cancer cells but stimulates the endometrium. Bleeding on tamoxifen therefore needs direct visualisation and biopsy, as ultrasound is unreliable because of benign thickening.

questions.stem: Which ultrasound finding in a pelvic mass is most suspicious for ovarian malignancy?

options.text: A multilocular cyst with solid areas, bilateral lesions and ascites
A unilocular, thin-walled cyst 3 cm in diameter in a premenopausal woman
A small follicular cyst that resolves on a repeat scan
A cyst with ground-glass echoes in an endometriosis patient with cyclical pain

questions.correctOptionText: A multilocular cyst with solid areas, bilateral lesions and ascites

distractorRationale.a: Correct: multilocularity, solid components, bilaterality and ascites all raise the ultrasound score.
distractorRationale.b: A simple unilocular cyst is almost always benign.
distractorRationale.d: Ground-glass echoes suggest an endometrioma, which is benign.

questions.explanation: Each of these features contributes to the ultrasound component of the Risk of Malignancy Index. Simple, thin-walled, unilocular cysts and functional cysts have a very low risk of malignancy.

questions.stem: A 62-year-old postmenopausal woman has a unilateral mass with solid areas on ultrasound (one ultrasound feature only, so U = 1) and a CA125 of 150 U/mL. Calculate her Risk of Malignancy Index (RMI = U x M x CA125).
questions.explanation: Postmenopausal status gives M = 3, so RMI = 1 x 3 x 150 = 450. This is above the usual threshold of 250 for high risk, so she should be referred to the gynaecological oncology MDT even though only one ultrasound feature is present.

questions.stem: A 22-year-old has a 14 cm solid-cystic adnexal mass found on ultrasound. In addition to CA125, which tumour markers should be measured first?

options.text: AFP, beta-hCG and LDH
CEA and CA19-9 only
PSA and CA15-3
No markers are indicated at this age

distractorRationale.a: Correct: these are the markers of germ cell tumours, which are the likely malignancies in young women.
distractorRationale.b: CEA and CA19-9 are used for mucinous and gastrointestinal tumours but are not first-line here.
distractorRationale.c: PSA is a prostate marker and CA15-3 a breast marker.
distractorRationale.d: Tumour markers are important in young women with complex masses.

questions.explanation: Malignant ovarian masses in young women are often germ cell tumours, which secrete AFP, hCG or LDH. Measuring these markers aids diagnosis, guides treatment and helps monitor response.

questions.stem: Which statement best explains why most ovarian cancers are diagnosed at an advanced stage?

options.text: Symptoms are vague and mimic benign conditions, the tumour spreads early across the peritoneum, and no effective screening test exists
Ovarian cancer always causes severe pain early in the disease
It is detected reliably by a cervical smear
It grows only in the endometrium, making sampling difficult

questions.correctOptionText: Symptoms are vague and mimic benign conditions, the tumour spreads early across the peritoneum, and no effective screening test exists

distractorRationale.a: Correct: non-specific symptoms, early transcoelomic spread and the lack of a screening test cause late diagnosis.
distractorRationale.c: Cervical screening does not detect ovarian cancer.
distractorRationale.d: Ovarian cancer arises in the ovary or fallopian tube, not the endometrium.

questions.explanation: Early ovarian cancer produces only vague symptoms such as bloating and early satiety, which are attributed to bowel or ageing problems. Meanwhile, cells shed into the peritoneal cavity and implant on peritoneal surfaces, and no screening test has been shown to reduce mortality.

questions.stem: True or false: a national screening programme using annual CA125 testing in all postmenopausal women is established practice because it reduces deaths from ovarian cancer.

options.text: True
False

questions.explanation: Population screening for ovarian cancer with CA125 and ultrasound has not been shown to reduce mortality, and CA125 is non-specific, raising false positives that lead to unnecessary surgery. Hence there is no general population screening programme, and early recognition of symptoms is emphasised.

questions.stem: A 55-year-old woman has had persistent abdominal bloating, early satiety and urinary frequency for 3 months. Her GP has tried treatment for irritable bowel syndrome without benefit. Explain why delayed diagnosis is common in ovarian cancer and outline how you would assess her.
markingGuide: Reasons for late diagnosis: non-specific symptoms mimic benign conditions such as IBS, deep pelvic location, early transcoelomic spread, no effective screening test
Persistent new symptoms in a woman over 50 should prompt consideration of ovarian cancer
History: family history of breast, ovarian or bowel cancer (BRCA, Lynch), weight loss, bowel changes
Examination: abdominal distension, ascites, pelvic mass, supraclavicular nodes
Investigations: CA125 and pelvic ultrasound, then calculate RMI
RMI above 250 leads to referral to a gynaecological oncology MDT; staging CT of the abdomen and pelvis
Mention biopsy or surgery for histological diagnosis, and consider genetic testing
questions.explanation: Early ovarian cancer behaves like a benign abdominal complaint, so persistence of new symptoms in an older woman is the key signal. A structured assessment with CA125, ultrasound and the RMI directs women to specialist care promptly.

questions.stem: A 70-year-old nulliparous woman with type 2 diabetes and a BMI of 38 presents with postmenopausal bleeding. Explain the pathophysiological link between her risk factors and endometrial cancer, and outline the investigations and treatment if cancer is confirmed.
markingGuide: Obesity increases peripheral conversion of androgens to oestrone in adipose tissue, giving unopposed oestrogen stimulation of the endometrium
Nulliparity and diabetes (hyperinsulinaemia) are further risk factors; type 1 endometrioid cancer is oestrogen-driven
Investigations: speculum and bimanual examination, TVUS endometrial thickness, hysteroscopy with biopsy
Staging imaging (MRI or CT) once cancer is confirmed
Treatment: total hysterectomy with bilateral salpingo-oophorectomy, with lymph node assessment in selected cases
Adjuvant radiotherapy or chemotherapy depending on stage, grade and histology
Early presentation due to bleeding explains the good prognosis
questions.explanation: Unopposed oestrogen drives endometrial proliferation, hyperplasia and eventually cancer, and obesity is the main source of it after menopause. Tissue diagnosis guides staging and surgery, and early detection through bleeding accounts for the high cure rate.
